title: The serotonin theory of depression: a systematic umbrella review of the evidence
authors: Moncrieff J, Cooper RE, Stockmann T, Amendola S, Hengartner MP, Horowitz MA
population: 17 systematic reviews, meta-analyses and large data-set analyses on serotonin and 5-HIAA concentrations, 5-HT1A receptor and SERT binding, tryptophan depletion and SERT gene associations in depression, searched to December 2020
funder: There was no specific funding for this review. MAH is supported by a Clinical Research Fellowship from North East London NHS Foundation Trust (NELFT). This funder had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report.
authorConflicts: MAH reported being co-founder, in April 2022, of a company aiming to help people safely stop antidepressants in Canada; MPH reported book royalties from Palgrave Macmillan; JM reported royalties for books about psychiatric drugs, NIHR grants outside the submitted work and unpaid positions in the Critical Psychiatry Network and the Council for Evidence-based Psychiatry; TS is co-chairperson of the Critical Psychiatry Network; RC is an unpaid board member of the International Institute for Psychiatric Drug Withdrawal; SA declared no conflicts.
result: Two meta-analyses of 5-HIAA (largest n=1002) showed no association with depression; a meta-analysis of cohort studies of plasma serotonin (n=1869) showed no relationship with depression; 5-HT1A receptor and SERT binding studies gave weak and inconsistent evidence; tryptophan depletion had no effect in most healthy volunteers, with weak evidence of an effect in those with a family history of depression (n=75); the largest SERT gene studies (n=115,257 and n=43,165) found no association with depression and no gene-stress interaction. The authors concluded that the main areas of serotonin research provide no consistent evidence of an association between serotonin and depression.
